Command line flag (--model or -m) 2. The model key in the config file 3. The last used model 4. The first model using an internal priority'; variants example and `variant_cycle` keybind. docs/config (2026-09-21): `small_model` 'a separate model for lightweight tasks like title generation'; `disabled_providers`, `enabled_providers`; provider `timeout`, `headerTimeout`, `chunkTimeout`, `setCacheKey`. docs/zen (2026-09-21): 'There are a large number of models out there but only a few of these models work well as coding agents'; 'benchmarked the combination of the model/provider'. ggprompts (secondary, 2026-09-21): 'Built-in Snapshot (models-snapshot) from compile time... Live fetch from models.dev API'. models.dev (2026-09-21): 'An open-source database of AI models' with context window, output length, reasoning, tool calls, pricing per model; providers include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, Alibaba, DeepSeek, Mistral.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: Requirements 4-5. JevCode today has only Anthropic and OpenRouter generator providers (src/provider/anthropic.ts, openrouter.ts) and a Jev provider switch (typesafe native vs OpenRouter decisions endpoint per .env.example). Build one `src/provider/catalog.ts`: bundle a models.dev `api.json` snapshot at build time, refresh in the background after first frame (never on the startup path), map env vars OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, FIREWORKS_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY to providers, and expose `provider/model` ids to a fuzzy picker in the TUI (search over id, name, context, price). INFERENCE: META_API_KEY has no first-class provider in the fetched docs; treat it as an OpenAI-compatible provider with a baseURL, and validate with one tiny request on `/connect`. Add a `small_model` slot (title, compaction summary) and use the catalogue's `limit.context/output` for the context meter and `usable()`. Keep TypeSafe/Jev out of this catalogue entirely: Jev is the decider with a pinned dated id and must not be selectable as a generator. Ship a short curated 'recommended for coding' list (Zen-style) rather than surfacing all 75 providers by default.

mechanisms.name: Bounded steps with a graceful final step, plan-mode reminders, and last-step tool removal
mechanisms.what: `steps` caps model iterations per agent; on the last step the runner removes tools and appends an assistant-role `MAX_STEPS_PROMPT` so the model lands with a text summary; new user input resets the allowance. The session loop continues while `finish === 'tool-calls'`, checks `compaction.isOverflow` before each turn, and applies `SessionReminders` that inject plan-mode text (`PLAN_MODE`, `PROMPT_PLAN`) or, after switching plan->build, 'A plan file exists at <path>. You should execute on the plan defined within it'; plan-enter/plan-exit tools flip the mode. Prompt parts are resolved concurrently (`Effect.forEach(..., { concurrency: 'unbounded' })`) and system prompt inputs (skills, env, instructions, MCP instructions, model messages) are gathered with `Effect.all`.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: A budget stop produces a handoff summary instead of an abrupt halt, which is exactly what resume needs; reminders make mode switches self-explanatory to the model without user prompting; concurrent assembly keeps per-turn overhead low.
mechanisms.evidence: v2 docs/agents (2026-09-21): 'steps sets a positive maximum number of model steps... OpenCode removes tools and asks the model to summarize in text. New user input resets the allowance'. Source session/prompt.ts (2026-09-21): `import { MAX_STEPS_PROMPT } from '@opencode-ai/core/session/runner/max-steps'`; `const maxSteps = agent.steps ?? Infinity; const isLastStep = step >= maxSteps`; `...(isLastStep ? [{ role: 'assistant', content: MAX_STEPS_PROMPT }] : [])`; `compaction.isOverflow({ tokens: lastFinished.tokens, model })`; `Effect.forEach(input.parts, resolvePart, { concurrency: 'unbounded' })`; `const [skills, env, instructions, mcpInstructions, modelMsgs] = yield* Effect.all([...])`. Source session/reminders.ts (2026-09-21): quoted BUILD_SWITCH text and PLAN_MODE placeholders; tool dir listing shows `plan.ts`, `plan-enter.txt`, `plan-exit.txt`.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode already has budgets (JEVCODE_MAX_STEPS, wall, spend; src/loop/budget.ts, stop.ts) and a persistent plan with evidence. Adopt the graceful last step: when any budget is about to fire, run one final generator call with the action set reduced to `done` and a request for a handoff summary, stored in the checkpoint and shown at the pause point (COORDINATION-DESIGN §7.2). Adopt reminders as code-inserted facts when the mode flips (jev-only vs llm-jev, paused vs resumed) so the generator never guesses state. Jev's completion Noul remains the decider of 'done'; the summary is just better input to it.

mechanisms.name: Extension seams: markdown custom commands with shell/file injection, file-named custom tools, and plugin hooks around tool execution, permissions and compaction
mechanisms.what: Commands: `.opencode/commands/*.md` with frontmatter `description`, `agent`, `model`, `subtask` (forces subagent execution); body uses `$ARGUMENTS`, `$1..$N`, `!`cmd`` shell output, and `@path` file inclusion. Custom tools: `.opencode/tools/<name>.ts` where 'The filename becomes the tool name' (multiple exports become `<filename>_<export>`), `tool({description, args: zod, execute(args, {agent, sessionID, messageID, directory, worktree})})`, may shell out to any language. Plugins: loaded from global/project config and `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`, `.opencode/plugins/` (npm installs via Bun into `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`); hooks include `tool.execute.before/after`, `permission.asked/replied`, `session.created/compacted/idle/status/error/diff`, `message.updated/part.updated`, `file.edited`, `lsp.client.diagnostics`, `shell.env`, `tui.prompt.append/command.execute/toast.show`, `experimental.session.compacting` (inject `output.context` or replace `output.prompt`).
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Repetitive prompts become one-keystroke templates with live shell context; teams add tools without touching the core; observability and policy hooks sit exactly at the tool boundary and the compaction boundary.
mechanisms.evidence: docs/commands (2026-09-21): `subtask` 'will force the agent to act as a subagent, even if mode is set to primary'; 'Commands run in your project's root directory and their output becomes part of the prompt'; '@' files 'The file content gets included in the prompt automatically'. docs/custom-tools (2026-09-21): 'The filename becomes the tool name'; 'Each export becomes a separate tool with the name <filename>_<exportname>'; context `{ agent, sessionID, messageID, directory, worktree }`. docs/plugins (2026-09-21): hook list as quoted; 'tool.execute.before enables intercepting and altering tool execution arguments before runtime'; 'experimental.session.compacting: Allows injecting context via output.context array or replacing entire compaction prompt via output.prompt'; 'Plugin tools with duplicate names override built-in equivalents'.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: Lower priority than the loop-side items, but cheap: JevCode's stages (src/loop/stages/{intent,context,propose,risk,execute,judge,complete,replan}.ts) are already discrete, so a `before/after` hook seam per stage is a small addition and gives the perf tooling (src/perf) and future policy plugins a stable surface. Markdown commands with `!`cmd`` injection fit the TUI command registry (src/tui/commands/registry.ts) and are a fast way for users to bring their existing workflows over during onboarding. Keep hooks synchronous-bounded with timeouts so a slow plugin cannot stall a step.

mechanisms.name: Experimental Code Mode: one `execute` tool runs a confined script over namespaced MCP tools instead of exposing every MCP schema
mechanisms.what: Behind `experimentalCodeMode`, the registry lazily imports `tool/code-mode.ts`, which builds a `server.tool` tree from connected MCP servers (`groupByServer`, `toolTree`) and exposes a single `execute` tool: 'Run a confined orchestration script with access to connected MCP tools.' Child tool calls still pass through `tool.execute.before/after` plugin hooks and permissions; MCP results are projected to text or attachments. Related: MCP config warns 'MCP servers add to your context, so you want to be careful with which ones you enable'; MCP tool fetch has a 5,000 ms timeout; servers can be `enabled: false` or enabled per agent only.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Collapses N tool schemas (which otherwise sit in every request) into one, and lets the model compose several MCP calls in one step; the per-agent MCP enablement is the non-experimental way to keep the context small today.
mechanisms.evidence: Source tool/code-mode.ts (2026-09-21): `export const CODE_MODE_TOOL = 'execute'`; DESCRIPTION quoted; `groupByServer`, `toolTree`, `invokeChildTool` calling `plugin.trigger('tool.execute.before', ...)`. Source tool/registry.ts (2026-09-21): `const codeMode = flags.experimentalCodeMode ? yield* Effect.promise(() => import('./code-mode')) : undefined`. docs/mcp-servers (2026-09-21): 'Timeout in ms for fetching tools from the MCP server. Defaults to 5000 (5 seconds)'; 'If you have a large number of MCP servers you may want to only enable them per agent and disable them globally'; GitHub MCP 'can easily exceed the context limit'. Marked EXPERIMENTAL upstream.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode has no MCP today and its generator proposes exactly one action per step, so this is a watch item, not a port. If MCP support is added, prefer per-agent enablement and lazy tool-schema loading over exposing all tools, and consider the one-program-tool shape. Do not adopt the experimental flag surface itself.

speed_tricks: Default in-process transport: the TUI starts the server in a worker thread and uses a fake URL (`http://opencode.internal`) plus an in-memory event source, so there is no socket or serialization hop unless `--port`/attach is requested (docs/research/tui/01-opencode.md §1 from R:packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui.ts, fetched 2026-09-20; docs/server fetched 2026-09-21).

Coalesce bus events for 16 ms and flush inside one batched store update so a burst of message.part.updated events yields a single render (local note §1 from R:packages/tui/src/context/sdk.tsx, 2026-09-20). JevCode's Ink renderer can do the same with a 16 ms flush in useEngine.
Fire-and-forget prompts (`POST /session/:id/prompt_async` -> 204) with progress on the SSE stream; never block a client on a model turn (docs/server, 2026-09-21).

Prune before you summarize: erase tool outputs older than the last 40k protected tokens when that frees >20k, and only then pay for an LLM compaction; keep a 2k-15k verbatim tail; truncate tool outputs to 2,000 chars in the summarizer's input (session/compaction.ts, 2026-09-21).
Model-aware overflow threshold `usable = input_limit - min(20k, maxOutput)` or `context - maxOutput` from catalogue limits; no fixed window (session/overflow.ts, 2026-09-21).

Spill large tool outputs (>2,000 lines or >50 KB) to a file and return a head/tail preview plus the path; 7-day cleanup; caps configurable via `tool_output.max_lines/max_bytes` (tool/truncate.ts, 2026-09-21).

Bounded reads: 2,000 lines default, 2,000-char line cap, 50 KB refusal without offset/limit; LSP warm-up forked in the background so a read never waits on a language server (tool/read.ts, 2026-09-21).

Fuzzy edit replacer ladder (trimmed lines, block anchors with 0.65 Levenshtein similarity, whitespace/indent/escape normalisation, trimmed boundaries, context-aware, multi-occurrence) recovers whitespace-drift edits in code instead of spending a model round trip (tool/edit.ts, 2026-09-21).

Shadow git-dir snapshots share objects with the user's repo via `objects/info/alternates` and copy its index so nothing is re-hashed; skip untracked files >2 MiB; `snapshot: false` for huge repos (snapshot/index.ts; docs/config, 2026-09-21).
Run formatters automatically after each write/edit, detected from project markers, so no step is ever spent on formatting (docs/formatters, 2026-09-21).

Static allow/deny permission patterns evaluated on a parsed command (tree-sitter bash/PowerShell grammars, cwd tracking) so common commands skip any interactive or model-based check (docs/permissions; tool/shell.ts, 2026-09-21). For JevCode: allow-listed commands skip the Jev risk call.

LSP off by default; when on, servers spawn lazily per file extension with de-duplicated in-flight spawns; the docs themselves recommend CLI lint/typecheck instead because LSP servers 'slow down agent workflows' (docs/lsp; lsp/lsp.ts, 2026-09-21).

Lazy skills: only `name`+`description` are in context; bodies load via the `skill` tool on demand, and skill outputs are exempt from pruning so they are never re-loaded (docs/skills; compaction.ts, 2026-09-21).
`small_model` for titles and summaries so the expensive generator is not used for housekeeping (docs/config, 2026-09-21).

Model catalogue as compile-time snapshot with live models.dev refresh afterwards; `whitelist`/`enabled_providers` shrink what the picker has to search (docs/providers, docs/config; ggprompts secondary, 2026-09-21).

Background subagents (experimental flag) return immediately with explicit 'do not sleep, poll, or duplicate' instructions; depth cap 1 by default; `task_id` resumes a specialist's session instead of re-priming it (tool/task.ts, 2026-09-21).
MCP: 5 s tool-fetch timeout, `enabled: false` to park a server, enable per agent rather than globally to keep tool schemas out of every request (docs/mcp-servers, 2026-09-21).
Concurrent assembly of per-turn inputs (`Effect.all` over skills/env/instructions/MCP instructions/messages; `concurrency: 'unbounded'` for prompt part resolution) (session/prompt.ts, 2026-09-21).
TUI keeps at most 100 messages per session in memory and drops the oldest (local note §1 from R:packages/tui/src/context/sync.tsx, 2026-09-20).

Provider transport knobs exposed in config: `timeout`, `headerTimeout`, `chunkTimeout`, `setCacheKey` (docs/config, 2026-09-21) - JevCode already has idle timeouts and jittered retries; add cache-key control for prompt caching.
pitfalls: Fuzzy edit replacers can silently apply to the wrong block: a single BlockAnchor candidate is accepted at only 0.65 average similarity, and only the multiple-match case throws (tool/edit.ts, 2026-09-21). Record which replacer fired, show it in the diff view, and keep JevCode's unique-occurrence rule as the hard error.

LSP integration costs memory and latency and drifts out of sync; opencode's own docs say so and recommend CLI diagnostics instead (docs/lsp, 2026-09-21). Do not add language servers to a harness with a 300 ms first-frame budget.

Snapshots on large repositories cost disk and indexing time; the docs tell users to disable them (docs/config, 2026-09-21). Copying the user's index into a shadow git dir must be read-only with respect to the user's `.git`; never write to it (JevCode's sandbox already write-denies `.git/config` and hooks).

Compaction config semantics changed between v1 (`prune`, `reserved`) and v2 (`auto`, `keep.tokens`, `buffer`) (v2 docs/compaction and docs/config disagree, 2026-09-21); a wrong `limit.context`/`limit.input` in the catalogue makes compaction fire on empty sessions (public issue anomalyco/opencode #27315 surfaced by WebSearch 2026-09-21, not fetched). Treat catalogue limits as data to validate, and never let compaction depend on a network fetch.
MCP servers 'add to your context'; GitHub MCP 'can easily exceed the context limit' (docs/mcp-servers, 2026-09-21). If JevCode adds MCP, enable per agent and lazily.

Background subagents are experimental and env-flag gated (`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_BACKGROUND_SUBAGENTS=true`, tool/task.ts, 2026-09-21); the parent is instructed not to poll, so a reliable completion-delivery path is required (JevCode: `Engine.deliver`, COORDINATION-DESIGN §5.4) or results are lost.

Subagent permission derivation copies only the parent's deny and external_directory rules, not its allows (agent/subagent-permissions.ts, 2026-09-21); users expect inheritance both ways. Document the rule in the TUI when a child is spawned.

The `doom_loop` guard is identical-input x3 only (docs/permissions, 2026-09-21) and misses semantically equivalent loops; JevCode's signature-based detector (src/loop/loopdetect.ts) is stronger; do not regress to the simpler rule.

Sharing uploads the full conversation to a public URL (`opncd.ai/s/<id>`; docs/share, 2026-09-21); default is manual, teams set `share: 'disabled'`. JevCode: keep 'no secrets in any artefact' and never upload; offer local `/export` only.
Remote `instructions` URLs are fetched with a 5 s timeout (docs/rules, 2026-09-21) - network on the startup path violates JevCode's zero-network first frame; defer or reject.

Two doc trees exist (`/docs/` v1 and `/v2/docs/` v2) with different agents (Scout in v1 search snippets, 'V2 has no built-in scout agent' in v2) and different compaction keys; always cite which. `github.com/sst/opencode` is a redirect to `anomalyco/opencode`; some third-party writeups still describe the pre-move layout.

Third-party architecture writeups disagree on facts (14 vs '20+' built-in tools, 30+ vs 40+ LSP servers, Hono vs Effect layering); the repo has moved much of the core into `@opencode-ai/core` and Effect (e.g. `bus/index.ts` no longer exists at the path deepwiki cites, 404 on 2026-09-21). Prefer the raw source on branch `dev` over gists/deepwiki.

OpenTUI (SolidJS + Zig over Bun FFI) and Bun are not portable to JevCode's Node 22 + Ink constraint (local note REJECT section, 2026-09-20); copy patterns (event coalescing, message caps, keybind schema), not code.

`steps` last-step behaviour removes tools and asks for a text summary (v2 docs/agents, 2026-09-21); if the summary itself is long it can push the session over the limit - pair it with the pre-turn overflow check.

Tool-output spill files persist for 7 days under the data dir (tool/truncate.ts, 2026-09-21); in JevCode they must go through core/redact.ts and live inside the run dir so secrets never land in a long-lived cache.

Bash permission patterns match the parsed command, so `'grep'` does not allow `grep foo file` while `'grep *'` does (docs/permissions, 2026-09-21); allow-list UX must show the pattern that matched or users will misconfigure it.

Research topic: SWE-bench Verified / SWE-bench Pro / Terminal-Bench leaderboards as of 2026 — which OPEN-SOURCE scaffolds lead and which mechanisms their write-ups credit. All fetches 2026-09-21 unless stated; read-only on <repo>; no keys printed. Items marked [INFERENCE] are my reading, not a cited claim; [SECONDARY] marks aggregator sites that report vendor/model numbers rather than an official scaffold board.

LEADERBOARD STATE (what could actually be fetched):

1. SWE-bench Verified. The official board https://www.swebench.com/verified.html is JS-rendered (fetched 2026-09-21: page text only, no table); the GitHub listing https://github.com/SWE-bench/experiments/tree/main/evaluation/verified (fetched 2026-09-21) shows dated scaffold dirs (latest visible 20250629_deepswerl_r2eagent_tts; names embed openhands, sweagent, Refact, trae, agentless, moatless, patchpilot, cortexa) — listing likely truncated. Epoch AI (https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-verified, fetched 2026-09-21) documents its v2.0.0 Feb-2026 scaffold upgrade: "a simple loop", tools = bash + Anthropic text_editor + OpenAI apply_patch, limits raised to "2M uncached read/write tokens and 20M cached token reads", Claude Code and Codex added via Inspect-SWE, results "improved significantly". Open-scaffold numbers with URL evidence: Live-SWE-agent board (https://live-swe-agent.github.io/, last entry 2025-12-12): Claude Opus 4.5 79.2% ($0.86/inst), Gemini 3 Pro 77.4% ($0.48), Claude Sonnet 4.5 75.4% ($0.68), GPT-5.2 73.6% ($0.55), Kimi K2 Thinking (open weights) 59.8% ($0.40), all "temperature=1 and high reasoning effort", no test-time scaling. SWE-Doctor paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00990, fetched 2026-09-21), five 2026 backbones, all on mini-SWE-agent base: mini-SWE-agent avg 73.7% (GPT-5.4 76.8, MiMo-V2.5-Pro 75.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro 75.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6 73.6, GPT-5.4-mini 67.4); live-SWE-agent avg 71.8%; SWE-Doctor avg 75.7% (best single 78.2% MiMo-V2.5-Pro). Confucius Code Agent (https://arxiv.org/html/2512.10398): 74.6% with Claude 4 Sonnet vs OpenHands 72.8% same backbone. mini-SWE-agent README (https://github.com/swe-agent/mini-swe-agent): ">74% on SWE-bench verified". [SECONDARY, from WebSearch snippets only, not fetched] vendor-scaffold model numbers up to ~93.9% (Claude Mythos Preview) and ~95% (llm-stats) — these are proprietary harnesses (Claude Code/Codex) and not comparable to the open-scaffold figures above.

2. SWE-bench Pro (public set, 731 tasks / 41 repos). Scale board https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public (fetched 2026-09-21): the top five entries all use the mini-swe-agent harness — Muse Spark 1.1 61.50±3.10, gpt-5.4 (xHigh) 59.10±3.56, Muse Spark 55.00±3.60, claude-opus-4-6 (thinking) 51.90±3.61, gemini-3.1-pro (thinking) 46.10±3.60; older rows use SWE-agent (claude-opus-4-5 45.89, claude-4-5-Sonnet 43.60, gpt-5 41.78, qwen3-coder-480b 38.70). Papers: SWE-Doctor avg 59.4% (GPT-5.4 65.4%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 59.8%) vs mini-SWE-agent avg 50.5%; CCA 59.0% (GPT-5.2), 54.3% (Claude 4.5 Opus), 52.7% (Claude 4.5 Sonnet); Live-SWE-agent 45.8% (Claude Sonnet 4.5, $0.73). So the open-scaffold frontier on Pro is a mini-SWE-agent-derived loop plus reproduction-test diagnosis (SWE-Doctor) or hierarchical memory + sub-agents (CCA).

3. Terminal-Bench. Official https://www.tbench.ai/leaderboard (and /terminal-bench/2.0) are JS-rendered — headers only (RANK/MODEL/AGENT/RESOLUTION RATE/COST/TOKENS), no rows (fetched 2026-09-21); the site now defaults to Terminal-Bench 4.0. [SECONDARY] TB 2.0 via https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/terminal-bench-2 ("Last updated September 22, 2026", 53 models): GPT-5.5 0.827, Claude Mythos Preview 0.820, Claude Sonnet 5 0.804, GPT-5.3 Codex 0.773; top open-weights model GLM-5.1 0.690 (rank 11). [SECONDARY] TB 2.1 via https://snorkel.ai/leaderboard/terminal-bench-2-1/ (fetched 2026-09-21, 89 tasks): GPT-6 Astra / Codex CLI 87.4±0.9 (2026-09-03), Claude Fable 5 / Claude Code 83.8±1.2, GPT-5.5 / Codex CLI 83.1±1.1, Claude Fable 5 / Terminus 2 (open-source) 80.4±1.2, Grok 4.5 / Cursor CLI 79.3±1.5 — i.e. the best open scaffold (Terminus 2) trails the vendor CLIs by ~3.4 points on the same model. [SECONDARY] TB 4.0 via https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/terminal-bench-4 (updated 2026-09-21, 66 tasks, Terminus 2 harness by default, 8-hour limit, avg@3): GPT-6 Astra 57.07% (~$8.21/task), Claude Fable 5.1 49.49%, Claude Opus 5 45.45%; Claude Opus 4.8 16.16% at $28.31/task. The Efficient Benchmarking paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23749v1) records the TB 2.0 board as "89 tasks, 101 agents across 23 scaffolds". Tmax paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.23321): Terminus-2 36.4±2.2 vs their mini-SWE-agent-with-persistent-shell harness 41.9±2.7 for the same Qwen baseline — the harness alone is worth ~5 points.

WHO LEADS AMONG OPEN SCAFFOLDS (2026): mini-SWE-agent is the de-facto standard base (Scale's standardized Pro runs, Live-SWE-agent, SWE-Doctor, SWE-Replay, Tmax, RTV all build on it); the leading open write-ups layer exactly one or two mechanisms on it: reproduction tests + runtime diagnosis (SWE-Doctor), runtime tool synthesis (Live-SWE-agent), hierarchical memory/compaction + sub-agents (CCA), and test-time scaling via verifiers, step-pruning, replay, or summary-voting (OpenHands critic, SWE-RM, SWE-TRACE, SWE-Replay, RTV/PDR, TRAE). For terminals, Terminus 2 (single tmux tool) is the reference open agent; vendor CLIs lead it by a few points.

FETCH GAPS: tbench.ai and swebench.com tables (JS), morphllm agent ranking and Artificial Analysis TB 2.1 (HTTP 429 / classifier rate-limit), mini-swe-agent FAQ cost/step defaults (page lacked them), Harbor Terminus-2 doc (redirected). Nothing was filled in from memory; the repo's existing docs/research/04-benchmarks-and-harnesses.md (fetched 2026-09-19) already holds Terminus 2 constants and SWE-agent cache_control details and is cited where I rely on it.

mechanisms.name: Minimal bash-only, single-action, linear-history base loop (mini-SWE-agent standard)
mechanisms.what: The agent has one tool (bash), emits exactly one action per step, appends every step to a strictly linear message list, and runs each action as an independent subprocess (no persistent shell state). Roughly 100 lines of agent code; no tool-calling API required.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It is now the standardized harness on Scale's SWE-bench Pro board (all top-5 rows), the base of every 2026 open write-up that beats it (Live-SWE-agent, SWE-Doctor, SWE-Replay, Tmax, RTV), and scores >74% on Verified by itself. Linear history makes the trajectory trivially checkpointable, replayable, and cache-friendly; independent subprocesses remove 'did the command finish?' ambiguity and crashed-shell failures.
mechanisms.evidence: README (fetched 2026-09-21): 'Does not have any tools other than bash — it doesn't even need to use the tool-calling interface of the LMs'; 'Has a completely linear history — every step of the agent just appends to the messages'; 'Executes actions with subprocess.run — every action is completely independent (as opposed to keeping a stateful shell session running)'; 'scores >74% on SWE-bench verified'. FAQ https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/faq/ (fetched 2026-09-21): subprocess design avoids ambiguity about command completion, crashed sessions, interrupt issues. Scale SWE-bench Pro board https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public (fetched 2026-09-21): ranks 1-5 (61.50, 59.10, 55.00, 51.90, 46.10) all 'mini-swe-agent' harness. Epoch AI https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-verified (fetched 2026-09-21): 'a fairly simple prompt, close to that used in the SWE-bench developers' bash-only runs'. Tmax https://arxiv.org/html/2606.23321 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'a simple harness based on mini-SWE-agent with persistent shell', '64 maximum tool calls', '120 s' per command; Terminus-2 36.4±2.2 vs this harness 41.9±2.7 on the same Qwen model.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode already has the one-Proposal-per-step contract (edit|write|patch|run|read|done) and a `sh -c` sandbox with a 120 s default timeout (docs/STATUS.md), so it is structurally a mini-SWE-agent-class loop. Keep it that way: do not grow the generator's tool surface; keep the transcript linear so checkpoints (steps.jsonl) double as replay archives (mechanism 7). [INFERENCE] A stable system-prompt prefix plus linear appends is what makes prompt caching effective; SWE-agent's default.yaml uses cache_control for this (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19). Jev is not on this path at all — the loop runs identically with the stub decider (llm-sieve arm), which is exactly the 'not mission-critical' property the user asked for.

mechanisms.name: Reproduce-first: bug-reproduction tests + runtime diagnosis records before patching (SWE-Doctor; Refact explore→reproduce→solve→check; Agentless)
mechanisms.what: Extract behavioural requirements from the issue, generate one targeted reproduction test per requirement, run each under a debugger (pdb/Delve), and only accept a 'diagnosis record' (fault location, runtime symptom, propagation path, fix direction) when runtime evidence was actually collected; patch generation is then guided by requirements + localization + diagnosis, with a completeness check that every stated behaviour was addressed.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It is the largest open-scaffold gain reported in 2026 on the hard benchmark: +8.9 points average on SWE-bench Pro and +2.0 on Verified over the same mini-SWE-agent base across five backbones, without any training. Reproduction-before-repair also converts 'does it work?' from a model opinion into an executable fact, which is exactly where a cheap judge is reliable.
mechanisms.evidence: SWE-Doctor HTML (fetched 2026-09-21): base = mini-SWE-agent; 'For each extracted requirement, SWE-Doctor uses an LLM to generate a targeted BRT'; debugger PDB (Python) / Delve (Go); 'accepts a diagnosis only when the agent has collected runtime evidence'. Verified avg: mini 73.7% → SWE-Doctor 75.7% (GPT-5.4 76.8→77.5; Claude Sonnet 4.6 73.6→75.5; MiMo-V2.5-Pro 75.5→78.2). Pro avg: 50.5% → 59.4% (GPT-5.4 55.1→65.4; Claude Sonnet 4.6 45.8→59.8). Cost per issue: $0.43 vs mini $0.23 (Verified); $0.64 vs $0.52 (Pro). Refact blog https://refact.ai/blog/2025/open-source-sota-on-swe-bench-verified-refact-ai/ (fetched 2026-09-21): 'Step 1: Explore the Problem → Step 2: Reproduce the Problem using debug_script() → Step 3: Make a Plan → Step 4: Check and Improve Your Work by running tests'; debug_script() uses pdb; 352/500 = 70.4% on 2025-05-15. Agentless https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'localization, repair, and patch validation' with reproduction + regression tests + majority voting; 32.00% Lite at $0.70.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode's design already lists 'regression/reproduction tests feeding the judge' and the llm-jev design says an LLM-written reproduction never satisfies the completion fact (docs/LLM-JEV-DESIGN.md §2.7). Add a code-owned 'reproduce' stage that runs BEFORE propose: generator writes one small failing test per requirement, the sandbox runs it, and code records the diagnosis record (failing assertion, traceback frames, touched files) as evidence attached to the Plan. Jev's measured role fits exactly here — 'reproduction judgment on code-extracted snippets (18/23)' and 'localisation from failure evidence (gold file #1 23/30, top-5 28/30)' — i.e. Jev ranks which traceback frame/file is the fault, it does not write or run anything. Speed: cost ~1.9x on Verified, so gate it: [INFERENCE] run the BRT stage only when the task has no existing failing test (a code fact) and cap it at 2-3 steps.

mechanisms.name: Hybrid verifier best-of-N: execution filters first, learned/LLM critic second, small N (OpenHands critic; R2E-Gym; SWE-RM; TRAE)
mechanisms.what: Sample N candidate trajectories/patches, drop any that fail regression or reproduction tests (execution-based filter), deduplicate the survivors by normalized AST/diff, then rank the remaining ones with an execution-free verifier (trained critic or LLM/selector votes) and return the top. TRAE adds early consensus (return as soon as ⌈N/2⌉ votes agree) and caps the selector at 30 tool rounds.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Each verifier type alone saturates; combined they keep scaling: R2E-Gym reports execution-only and execution-free verifiers each plateau at 42-43% while the hybrid reaches 51%. OpenHands: 60.6% → 66.4% with 5 attempts and a 32B critic. SWE-RM (3B-active MoE critic): 51.6→62.0 and 67.0→74.6 at RM@32. TRAE: Pass@1 rises monotonically N=1→10 (+5.83 to +14.60) while baselines degrade, because dedup + regression filtering removes the noise that fools pure voting.
mechanisms.evidence: OpenHands blog 2025-04-17 (fetched 2026-09-21): critic = 'Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct 32B' with 'a regression head on top of the last layer' and 'a temporal difference (TD) learning objective'; 'from 60.6% on a single trajectory rollout to 66.4% with five attempts'. R2E-Gym https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07164 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'Test-based verifiers suffer from low distinguishability, while execution-free verifiers are biased and often rely on stylistic features'; 'each approach individually saturates around 42-43% ... our approach achieves 51%'. SWE-RM https://arxiv.org/html/2512.21919 (fetched 2026-09-21): base 'Qwen3-30B-A3B', generative YES/NO classifier, score exp(ly)/(exp(ly)+exp(ln)); RM@32: Qwen3-Coder-Flash '51.6% to 62.0%', Qwen3-Coder-Max '67.0% to 74.6%'; trajectories from OpenHands and SWE-Agent. TRAE https://arxiv.org/html/2507.23370v1 (fetched 2026-09-21): unidiff-based dedup normalizing 'extra spaces, line breaks, and comments'; tester agent runs regression tests; selector does static review + generated unit tests; majority vote, 'if the first ⌈N/2⌉ votes are unanimous, this consensus patch is immediately returned'; N=3 Pass@1 62.27/66.40/59.00/65.67 (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Claude 3.7/GPT-4.1/Mixture) vs Augment 55.40/63.13/54.87/58.93; 'upper bound of 30 interaction rounds' for the selector.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: This is the shape JevCode's llm-jev 'Ledger+Sieve' already has: candidates run in shadow lanes against goal + regression tests (execution filter), and Jev is the execution-free ranker — measured 'arbitration among test-passing candidates from distinct behaviour clusters (gold-or-equivalent 10/10)' and 'ranking near-duplicate candidates ... top-3 40/40 at N ≤ 50'. Keep the order: code runs tests → code dedups by normalized diff → Jev ranks only survivors from distinct clusters → tests remain the arbiter. Use N=2-3, not 8-32; the papers' large-N gains come at multiplied cost and the user wants speed. Jev is off the critical path: with the stub decider the sieve falls back to 'first passing candidate' (llm-sieve arm).

mechanisms.name: Early stopping on a verifier confidence threshold instead of exhausting N (OpenHands 2026 verifier)
mechanisms.what: Run attempts sequentially; after each, score it; accept immediately when the score clears a threshold, otherwise sample another. Best-of-N reranking is kept only as the fallback when nothing clears.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It delivers most of the best-of-N gain at ~1.35 attempts on average instead of 8, which is the single biggest wall-clock/cost lever among the test-time-scaling methods. The same post shows critics trained only on benchmark traces are worse than random in production (AUC 0.45-0.48), so the threshold signal must come from something calibrated on real traces or from executed tests.
mechanisms.evidence: OpenHands blog 2026-03-05 (fetched 2026-09-21): two inference modes, 'Best-of-N Selection (rerank multiple attempts and pick the best)' and 'Early Stopping (accept as soon as the score clears a threshold)'; 'Best@8 73.8% vs Random@8 57.9%' on mixed-outcome instances; early stopping '+17.7 over random with 1.35 attempts on average'; benchmark-only critic 'only ~0.45-0.48 (worse than random)' vs production-trained 0.69 AUC using 'PR merge and code survival' signals.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode already has 'the tried-set instant verdict' and 'completion as a code fact' (LLM-JEV-DESIGN §2). Implement early stopping as: code fact (all goal tests newly pass, regression scope unchanged) → commit immediately, no further samples; only when zero candidates pass does the loop sample again, and only when several pass in distinct clusters does Jev arbitrate. Jev's confidence formula (Choice `(p_max − 1/n)/(1 − 1/n)`) is the threshold input, with the design's rule that no consumed decision sits at 0.5. [INFERENCE] Given the AUC finding, never let a Jev score alone accept a patch that has not executed; use it only to pick among executed passers or to decide 'sample once more vs stop'.

mechanisms.name: Per-step candidate pruning with a cheap guide (SWE-TRACE heuristic-guided TTS) instead of parallel full rollouts
mechanisms.what: At each step sample K candidate actions, score them with a cheap guide function against the task rubric, execute only the top-B (B=1 in low-latency mode), and continue — a beam of width 1-2 rather than N independent trajectories.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It beat full parallel rollouts on resolve rate while roughly halving wall-clock and cutting environment executions by 3x: 71.2% vs 69.9% for the same 30B model, 36.5 vs 63.8 minutes per issue, 128 vs 392 environment executions. It is the test-time-scaling variant designed for latency, which is what the user asked for.
mechanisms.evidence: SWE-TRACE HTML (fetched 2026-09-21): candidates 'a_{t,k} ~ π_θ(·|h̃_t)', scored 'u_t(a) = s_guide(h̃_t, a, R_x)', retained 'B_t = TopB(A_t, u_t(·)), B ≪ K'; 'In strict low-latency mode B=1, so only the single most promising action is executed'. Results: SWE-TRACE-30B 63.5%; + HG-TTS 71.2%; parallel rollout baseline 69.9% ('+1.3 points better ... while using substantially less wall-clock latency and far fewer environment executions'). Latency: parallel 63.8 min/issue vs heuristic-guided 36.5; environment executions 392 → 128. Training-side: shortest-path SFT cut tokens 37.2M → 26.3M (29.3%).
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: This is the most natural home for Jev: JevCode already asks Jev a Choice among concrete options (measured 'choosing among ≤ 255 concrete options when the right one is present (36/40 top-1 at N = 10)'). Sample 2-3 proposals per step from the generator in parallel, have Jev pick one BEFORE execution (a single decisions request, ~tens of ms per the design's latency budget of ≤15% of wall), execute only that one. If Jev is unavailable or low-confidence, code falls back to the first well-formed proposal — so the loop never blocks on Jev. Do not ask Jev to judge plans/intent (100% of jev-on's 223 refusals came from that, LLM-JEV-DESIGN §2.1); ask it to choose among concrete diffs/commands.

mechanisms.name: Replay/branching from archived trajectories instead of resampling from scratch (SWE-Replay)
mechanisms.what: Keep every prior attempt's trajectory; for each new attempt flip a coin (p=0.5) between exploring from scratch and branching from a 'critical intermediate step' of an archived trajectory. Steps are chosen by code heuristics: drop trajectories whose patch fails regression tests, group steps by the set of repository files explored so far (favour rare groups), and prefer steps with many reasoning paragraphs. Returning to a step is just applying a diff.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It matched or beat repeated sampling at 11-17% lower cost with 'negligible overhead', across mini-SWE-agent and Live-SWE-agent on Verified, Pro and Multilingual (Multilingual +7 points). It explicitly avoids LLM-as-judge and value models because 'they suffer from model miscalibration and fail to generalize to modern agents that synthesize custom bash scripts as tools'.
mechanisms.evidence: SWE-Replay HTML v2 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'The first run always generates a trajectory from scratch ... exploration and exploitation are treated as independent Bernoulli trials with probability p=0.5'; step selection = filter regression-failing patches → group by 'the set of repository files explored before that step' → 'the number of paragraphs in the reasoning content as a robust structural proxy' → softmax balancing. Verified: mini-SWE-agent + Gemini-2.5-Pro 60.2% vs 58.0%, $1.32 vs $1.52 (−13.2%); mini + Gemini-3-Pro 75.6% vs 75.4%, $2.38 vs $2.88 (−17.4%); Live-SWE-agent + Gemini-3-Pro 75.8% vs 75.6%, $2.59 vs $2.93. Pro 28.97% vs 28.73%; Multilingual 38.0% vs 31.0%, $1.11 vs $1.22. Overhead: 'only requires applying a diff file, which takes on the order of seconds'.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode already writes an atomic checkpoint every step (state.json, steps.jsonl) and supports `--resume <run-id>` — that is the archive. Add a 'branch from step k of run r' entry point to the engine (checkpoint/resume.ts) and use it in two places: (a) the replan stage, instead of restarting after loop detection, branch from the last step whose evidence still holds; (b) the bench's retry path. Choosing k is code (files-explored set + reasoning length) per the paper; [INFERENCE] Jev could additionally be asked a Choice among ≤10 candidate steps, but the paper's warning about miscalibrated judges argues for keeping code as the default and measuring Jev's marginal value in the §10.4 ablation before consuming it.

mechanisms.name: Vote over rollout summaries, and condition new attempts on distilled prior-attempt summaries (Recursive Tournament Voting / Parallel-Distill-Refine)
mechanisms.what: RTV: compress each rollout into a summary and pick a winner by recursive small-group comparisons of the summaries rather than full traces. PDR: when trying again, feed the new rollout a distilled summary of what earlier attempts tried and learned (sequential scaling).
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Reported on the two exact benchmarks in scope, both on open scaffolds: SWE-bench Verified (mini-SWE-agent) Claude 4.5 Opus 70.9% → 77.6%; Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Terminus 1) 46.9% → 59.1% — the largest Terminal-Bench gain in this set. Comparing summaries instead of traces keeps the judge prompt small and the comparison cheap.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv 2604.16529 abstract (fetched 2026-09-21): RTV 'recursively narrows a population of rollout summaries through small-group comparisons'; PDR 'conditioning new rollouts on summaries distilled from prior attempts'; 'SWE-Bench Verified (mini-SWE-agent) Claude-4.5-Opus improved from 70.9% to 77.6%'; 'Terminal-Bench v2.0 (Terminus 1) ... from 46.9% to 59.1%'. N values and cost are not in the abstract (full text not fetched).
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode's Plan-with-evidence and the replan Choice are already a PDR-shaped mechanism: on replan, the plan carries what was tried and why it failed. Make the distilled summary an explicit code-built artefact (tried-set, failing tests, files touched, last diagnosis record) that is prepended to the next attempt. For RTV, Jev's paired-comparison Choice among ≤255 options is the natural small-group comparator over summaries (never over full traces — Jev must not be asked to read long text). Cost stays low because summaries are a few hundred tokens and Jev is $0.042/M input tokens (LLM-JEV-DESIGN notation).

mechanisms.name: Runtime tool synthesis with a per-step reflection nudge (Live-SWE-agent)
mechanisms.what: Start from bash-only mini-SWE-agent; after every step append a fixed feedback message asking the model to 'reflect on the previous trajectories and decide if there are any tools you can create'; the model may write a Python/bash script into the environment and call it thereafter (mostly edit, view, search tools; sometimes domain analyzers).
mechanisms.why_it_helps: With late-2025 models it beat every open scaffold at almost no extra cost (Claude 4.5 Sonnet: 70.6% → 75.4% Verified, $0.56 → $0.68; Pro 45.8%), and ablations show both halves matter (no tool creation 62.0%, no reflection prompt 64.0%, full 76.0% on the subset). Caveat below: on mid-2026 backbones it no longer wins.
mechanisms.evidence: Live-SWE-agent HTML (fetched 2026-09-21): base 'mini-SWE-agent ... only access to bash tools'; reflection 'after each step' with prompt 'Reflect on the previous trajectories and decide if there are any tools you can create to help you with the current task'; tools = 'a script that can be executed in the environment'; Verified Claude 4.5 Sonnet mini 70.6%/$0.56 vs Live 75.4%/$0.68; Pro 45.8%/$0.73 vs SWE-agent 43.6%; ablation 62.0 / 64.0 / 76.0; 'edit, view, and search' dominate synthesized tools. Board https://live-swe-agent.github.io/ (fetched 2026-09-21): Opus 4.5 79.2% $0.86, Gemini 3 Pro 77.4% $0.48, Kimi K2 Thinking OSS 59.8% $0.40. Counter-evidence: SWE-Doctor table (fetched 2026-09-21) — live-SWE-agent avg 71.8% vs mini 73.7% on Verified with GPT-5.4/Claude Sonnet 4.6/DeepSeek-V4-Pro/MiMo-V2.5-Pro; SWE-Replay found Live-SWE-agent ≈ mini (75.8 vs 75.6) with Gemini-3-Pro.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: Cheap to add as an OPTIONAL `tool` action kind: the generator writes a script under the run's scratch dir, the risk stage scores it (Jev's harm Scores already gate unverified `run` commands), and later steps may invoke it. Ship it OFF by default for strong 2026 models and let the bench (jev-on vs jev-off arms) decide; [INFERENCE] its value is highest for weaker/cheaper generators (GLM-5.3-flash in llm-jev), where view/search/edit helpers reduce malformed edits (13-35% malformed at one sample per step, LLM-JEV-DESIGN §1.2). Jev's role is only the accept/deny risk score on the synthesized script — not mission-critical.

mechanisms.name: Hierarchical working memory + threshold-triggered compaction that preserves fixed categories, plus sub-agents and a meta-agent build-test-improve loop (Confucius Code Agent)
mechanisms.what: Keep a structured working memory (task goals, decisions, open TODOs, critical error traces) separate from raw history; when context nears a configurable threshold, an 'Architect' pass replaces marked old messages with a summary while keeping a rolling window of recent raw messages; decompose work to sub-agents with their own contexts; and use a meta-agent that synthesizes agent configs, drives them on regression tasks, and iteratively edits prompts/tool policies from observed failures.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Ablation on a 100-task SWE-bench Pro subset: no context management 42.0% / 44.0% → hierarchical memory + compression 48.6% / 51.6% (Claude 4 / 4.5 Sonnet), with a further 'large decline' when learned tool-use features are removed. Full system: 74.6% Verified (Claude 4 Sonnet) vs OpenHands 72.8% same backbone; Pro 52.7% (4.5 Sonnet), 54.3% (4.5 Opus), 59.0% (GPT-5.2). The meta-agent is the 'iterate on small tasks' loop the user asked for, automated.
mechanisms.evidence: CCA HTML (fetched 2026-09-21): compaction 'When the context length approaches configurable thresholds, the Architect Agent is invoked', 'replaces marked historical messages with this compressed summary while maintaining a rolling window of recent messages in their original form', summary 'explicitly preserves key information categories (e.g., task goals, decisions made, open TODOs, and critical error traces)'; meta-agent 'synthesizes agent configurations, wires together orchestrator components and extensions, evaluates candidate agents on representative tasks, and iteratively refines prompts and tool-use policies based on observed failures' and 'drives it on a suite of regression tasks'. Numbers: Verified 74.6% vs OpenHands 72.8%; Pro 52.7/54.3/59.0; ablation 42.0→48.6 and 44.0→51.6. Related: Terminus 2 `_summarize()` handoff at `target_free_tokens=4000` (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19).
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode's persistent Plan-with-evidence plus the bounded 4-step window (tokens flat at ~12k/step from step 1 to 25, docs/STATUS.md) is already a hierarchical-memory design. Two cheap additions: (1) make the compaction summary a code-built structured record with exactly CCA's four categories, sourced from harness facts (test counts, tried-set, last traceback) so no model has to write it — per the design principle that Jev never builds text; (2) point the meta-agent idea at the bench: the QuixBugs/ladder/SWE-30 suites and the six bench arms (src/bench/conditions.ts) are the 'regression tasks'; a script that flips one prompt/threshold at a time and reruns the 30-task subset is the meta-agent loop, no new model needed. Sub-agents map onto the existing shadow lanes (src/synth/sieve/lanes.ts) — spawn a lane per candidate with its own transcript rather than a shared context.

mechanisms.name: Repo map / hierarchical localization as the candidate set for file selection (Aider repo map; Agentless localization)
mechanisms.what: Build a compact, ranked map of the repository (symbols and signatures, ranked on a file-dependency graph) within a small token budget, and use it to decide which files to open, rather than letting the agent grep blindly; Agentless does the same as an explicit top-down phase (repo structure → files → functions → lines).
mechanisms.why_it_helps: It cuts the read/explore steps that dominate early trajectories and gives a ranker a concrete, bounded option list. Aider's default budget is only 1k tokens; Agentless reached SOTA-at-the-time on Lite with a fixed three-phase pipeline at $0.70 per issue, showing localization quality carries much of the result.
mechanisms.evidence: Aider repo map (fetched 2026-09-21): includes 'the most important classes and functions along with their types and call signatures'; 'a graph ranking algorithm, computed on a graph where each source file is a node and edges connect files which have dependencies'; 'The token budget is influenced by the --map-tokens switch, which defaults to 1k tokens'; 'it does expand the repo map significantly at times, especially when no files have been added to the chat'. Agentless https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'a simplistic three-phase process of localization, repair, and patch validation, without letting the LLM decide future actions', 32.00% Lite, $0.70. SWE-Doctor performs 'requirement-level bug localization before test generation' (fetched 2026-09-21).
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode's context stage already asks Jev Nouls over 'path-keyed candidate files (one request)' with measured localisation quality (gold file #1 23/30, top-5 28/30; function top-5 35/37; line top-3 36/40). What is missing is a good candidate generator: [INFERENCE] add a code-built repo map (grep/ctags-style symbol index ranked by import graph plus traceback-frame files from the diagnosis record), capped at ~1k tokens, as the option list Jev ranks. This keeps Jev off the mission-critical path — if Jev is unavailable, the top-k of the code ranking is used directly.

mechanisms.name: Single terminal tool with hard caps, summarize-and-handoff, and confirm-before-finish (Terminus 2 / Tmax terminal recipe)
mechanisms.what: Give the model one interactive tmux session (send keystrokes, read the screen), bound every command with a wait/timeout, cap tool calls and per-command time, never ask the user, summarize and hand off when context runs low, and require a second confirmation before declaring the task complete.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Terminus 2 is the reference open agent on Terminal-Bench and the default harness on vals.ai; with Claude Fable 5 it scores 80.4±1.2 on TB 2.1, within ~3.4 points of Claude Code on the same model. Tmax shows the harness itself is worth ~5 points on the same model (36.4 vs 41.9) and that persistent shell + interleaved thinking + '64 maximum tool calls' + '120 s' timeouts is a sufficient recipe.
mechanisms.evidence: tbench.ai/news/terminus (fetched 2026-09-21): 'Terminus has only a single tool at its disposal: an interactive tmux session running inside its execution environment'; 'Terminus will never ask for user input and will instead independently push to complete its task'. Snorkel TB 2.1 (fetched 2026-09-21): Claude Fable 5 / Terminus 2 80.4% ±1.2 vs Claude Fable 5 / Claude Code 83.8% ±1.2; vals.ai TB 4.0 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'Terminus 2 harness' default, 8-hour limit, avg@3. Tmax https://arxiv.org/html/2606.23321 (fetched 2026-09-21): 'a simple harness based on mini-SWE-agent with persistent shell', '64 maximum tool calls', '120 s' per bash command, preserved 'interleaved thinking'; Terminus-2 36.4±2.2 vs Tmax harness 41.9±2.7 (Qwen baseline). Terminus 2 constants — `min(parsed_cmd.duration, 60)`, double-confirm, `target_free_tokens=4000`, `_summarize` — from docs/research/04 (fetched 2026-09-19).
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: Already adopted in design: single `run` action, 120 s default / 600 s max timeout clamped to wall, 'confirm-before-finish as a Jev decision', 'summarize-and-handoff at context limit' (docs/RESEARCH.md §0.3). For the Terminal-Bench path (bench/terminalbench, Harbor installed-agent adapter) the missing piece is long-running/interactive commands: mini-style subprocess.run cannot drive REPLs or watch a server; [INFERENCE] add an optional persistent-shell sandbox mode with an explicit wait/duration argument (Terminus-style min(duration,60)) only for TB tasks, keep subprocess.run for SWE tasks. Jev's role: the 'is the task done?' double-confirm Noul, which is already a measured yes/no on code facts.

mechanisms.name: Stuck-detection guardrails: code-injected nudges, file-overload limits, and removing planners the model no longer needs (Refact.ai)
mechanisms.what: Detect off-track states with code (repeated failures, too many files requested, post-debug without reading files) and insert short helper messages ('Open all visited files using cat()', 'Now implement the solution above'); refuse folder dumps of >5 files and ask for one-by-one access; drop the separate o3 strategic-planning tool once the main model (Claude 4 Sonnet) could plan itself.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Refact's open pipeline moved from 70.4% to 74.4% on Verified with the model upgrade plus these simplifications, and the write-up credits guardrails for catching 'when the model is stuck or going off track' at pass@1 with temperature 0 — i.e. reliability without extra samples.
mechanisms.evidence: Refact blog (fetched 2026-09-21): helper messages 'inserted mid-run to redirect off-track reasoning, such as reminders to "Open all visited files using cat()" after debugging and "Now implement the solution above" after planning steps'; orchestration Claude 3.7, debug sub-agent Claude 3.7 + o4-mini, planner o3, 'Temperature: 0', 'Each task attempted only once (pass@1)', 352/500 (70.4%) on 2025-05-15. WebSearch snippet of the follow-up post https://refact.ai/blog/2025/1-agent-on-swe-bench-verified-using-claude-4-sonnet/ (not fetched, 2026-09-21): 74.40%; 'removed strategic_planning() (previously powered by o3)'; 'if a folder contains more than 5 files, the Agent returns an error and asks for one-by-one access'.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode has hashed loop detection (same command+result, patch hash, failure, unresolved intent ×3) → replan Choice, and 'bounded format-error re-queries'. Add Refact-style code nudges as the FIRST response to a detected loop (zero model/Jev cost), escalating to the Jev replan Choice only on the second trigger. The 'drop the planner' lesson maps directly onto LLM-JEV-DESIGN's finding that Jev must never judge plans/intent (source of all 223 refusals) and that GLM's output must be 'small, plan-free'.

mechanisms.name: Iterate on a mid-difficulty task subset (30-70% historical pass rate) instead of full benchmarks (Efficient Benchmarking of AI Agents)
mechanisms.what: Select only tasks whose historical pass rate across prior agents lies between 30% and 70%; evaluate new harness variants on that subset and compare ranks, not absolute scores.
mechanisms.why_it_helps: Cuts 44-70% of tasks (median 58%) while keeping rank fidelity under scaffold shift (leave-one-scaffold-out Spearman 0.87 avg / 0.92 best, Kendall τ 0.73 avg / 0.80 best, '90% of agent pairs are ranked correctly'). It was validated on exactly the two benchmarks in scope (Terminal-Bench 2.0: 89 tasks, 101 agents, 23 scaffolds; SWE-bench Verified via HAL: 50 tasks, 33 agents). This is the principled version of 'test on small stuff and iterate'.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv 2603.23749 HTML (fetched 2026-09-21): Mid-Range filter '30–70%', 'motivated by Item Response Theory'; 'typical task reduction ranges from 44% to 70%, with a median of 58%'; LOSO Spearman 0.92 best / 0.87 avg, Kendall 0.80 best / 0.73 avg; benchmarks include 'Terminal-Bench 2.0: 89 tasks, 101 agents across 23 scaffolds' and 'SWE-bench Verified (HAL): 50 tasks, 33 agents'; caveat 'approximately five to ten agents must be evaluated on the full benchmark before reduction becomes reliable'. Abstract: 'absolute score prediction degrades under this shift, while rank-order prediction remains stable'.
mechanisms.applicability_to_jevcode: JevCode's bench already uses a 30-task Verified subset and 10 TB tasks with a 66-task feasibility manifest. [INFERENCE] Re-pick the 30 Verified instances from the mid-range band using public per-instance results in https://github.com/SWE-bench/experiments (many scaffolds' results/ JSON are public — the 5-10 agent history requirement is satisfied by the repo), and for the 10 TB tasks prefer tasks with published 30-70% solve rates over 'feasible' ones. Report ranks between arms (jev-on/jev-off/jev-only/llm-jev/llm-sieve/jev-off-tuned), not absolute percentages — this matches the design's pre-registered discordant-pair criteria (LLM-JEV-DESIGN §1.3).

speed_tricks: Early-stop on the first candidate that is a code fact (all goal tests newly pass, regression scope unchanged); the OpenHands verifier post shows thresholded early stopping gets +17.7 over random at 1.35 attempts on average instead of N=8 (https://www.openhands.dev/blog/20260305-learning-to-verify-ai-generated-code, fetched 2026-09-21).

Prune per step, not per trajectory: sample 2-3 proposals, let Jev pick one before execution, execute only that one (SWE-TRACE B=1 mode cut wall from 63.8 to 36.5 min/issue and environment executions from 392 to 128 while beating parallel rollouts 71.2 vs 69.9, https://arxiv.org/html/2604.14820, fetched 2026-09-21).

Branch from an existing checkpoint instead of resampling from scratch: SWE-Replay's step return 'only requires applying a diff file, which takes on the order of seconds' and cut cost 11-17% at equal or better resolve rate (https://arxiv.org/html/2601.22129v2, fetched 2026-09-21). JevCode already checkpoints every step.

Filter before you rank: run regression/reproduction tests and drop failures, then dedup by normalized diff/AST (TRAE: unidiff parse, strip whitespace/comments; SWE-Replay: drop regression-failing trajectories) so the ranker (Jev) sees only a handful of distinct survivors (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.23370v1, fetched 2026-09-21).
Stop voting early: TRAE returns as soon as the first ⌈N/2⌉ selector votes are unanimous and caps the selector at 30 tool rounds (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.23370v1, fetched 2026-09-21).

Compare summaries, not traces: Recursive Tournament Voting narrows 'a population of rollout summaries through small-group comparisons' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16529, fetched 2026-09-21) — keeps every Jev/judge request a few hundred tokens.

Hard caps everywhere: 120 s per command and 64 tool calls (Tmax, https://arxiv.org/html/2606.23321, fetched 2026-09-21); Terminus 2 waits min(duration, 60) s per keystroke batch and hands off with a summary at target_free_tokens=4000 (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19); mini-SWE-agent ships a cost_limit per instance (docs/research/04). JevCode's 120 s / 600 s clamps and spend cap already match.

Keep the transcript linear with a stable prefix so prompt caching hits: mini-SWE-agent's 'completely linear history' (https://github.com/swe-agent/mini-swe-agent, fetched 2026-09-21); SWE-agent's default.yaml uses cache_control (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19); Epoch's v2 limits assume '20M cached token reads' vs 2M uncached (https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-verified, fetched 2026-09-21). [INFERENCE] the caching gain itself is not quantified by these sources.

Compact instead of restart: replace old messages with a structured summary holding task goals, decisions, open TODOs, critical error traces, keep a rolling window of recent raw messages (CCA, https://arxiv.org/html/2512.10398, fetched 2026-09-21); build that summary from harness facts in code so no model call is needed.

Reproduce once, reuse the diagnosis record: SWE-Doctor's runtime-grounded diagnosis (fault location, symptom, propagation path) is produced once and guides all later patch attempts (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00990, fetched 2026-09-21); [INFERENCE] cache it on the Plan so replans and replay branches do not re-run the debugger.

Ship a ranked repo map (~1k tokens, Aider default) as the option list for file selection so the agent spends fewer read/grep steps (https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html, fetched 2026-09-21); JevCode's context stage then ranks candidates in one Jev request.

Code-injected nudges before any model or Jev call when a loop is detected ('Open all visited files', 'Now implement the solution above' — Refact, https://refact.ai/blog/2025/open-source-sota-on-swe-bench-verified-refact-ai/, fetched 2026-09-21); zero-cost first response, Jev replan Choice only on the second trigger.

Drop separate planners when the generator can plan: Refact removed its o3 strategic_planning() tool with the Claude 4 Sonnet upgrade (WebSearch snippet of https://refact.ai/blog/2025/1-agent-on-swe-bench-verified-using-claude-4-sonnet/, 2026-09-21, not fetched); LLM-JEV-DESIGN independently found plan/intent judging was the source of all 223 Jev refusals.

Iterate on the 30-70% pass-rate band: 44-70% fewer tasks with ~0.87 Spearman rank fidelity under scaffold shift (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23749v1, fetched 2026-09-21); compare arms by rank/discordant pairs, not absolute score.

Keep Jev's share of wall bounded and off the critical path: JevCode's own gate is 'Jev share of synthMs + shell Jev time ≤ 15% of total wall' with a code default for every question (llm-sieve arm), so a Jev outage or rate limit degrades to a plain mini-SWE-agent-class loop rather than blocking.
pitfalls: Scores are scaffold-dependent and boards mix scaffolds: the same Qwen model scores 36.4±2.2 on Terminus-2 vs 41.9±2.7 on Tmax's harness (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.23321, fetched 2026-09-21); Claude Fable 5 scores 83.8 on Claude Code vs 80.4 on Terminus 2 (https://snorkel.ai/leaderboard/terminal-bench-2-1/, fetched 2026-09-21); Scale's Pro board mixes mini-swe-agent and SWE-agent rows (fetched 2026-09-21). Never compare JevCode against vendor-CLI numbers; compare against mini-SWE-agent on the same model and instances.

Runtime tool synthesis (Live-SWE-agent) is model-dependent and regressed on 2026 backbones: avg 71.8% vs mini-SWE-agent 73.7% on Verified and 51.4% vs 50.5% on Pro across GPT-5.4 / Claude Sonnet 4.6 / DeepSeek-V4-Pro / MiMo-V2.5-Pro (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00990, fetched 2026-09-21), and only ≈ parity with Gemini-3-Pro (https://arxiv.org/html/2601.22129v2). Ship it off by default and measure.

Execution-free verifiers are biased and saturate: 'biased and often rely on stylistic features', each verifier type alone plateaus at 42-43% (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07164, fetched 2026-09-21); benchmark-trained critics score AUC 0.45-0.48 in production, worse than random (https://www.openhands.dev/blog/20260305-learning-to-verify-ai-generated-code, fetched 2026-09-21). Jev must rank only executed, test-passing candidates from distinct behaviour clusters, never accept an unexecuted patch — consistent with JevCode's 'tests are the arbiter' principle.

Best-of-N multiplies cost and is disallowed or separately flagged on boards: Live-SWE-agent reports 'without test-time scaling' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13646); the SWE-bench experiments repo names TTS variants separately (e.g. 20250629_deepswerl_r2eagent_tts, Skywork-SWE-32B+TTS_Bo8; fetched 2026-09-21). Keep N ≤ 3 and report N.

Reproduction-first roughly doubles per-issue cost on the easy benchmark: SWE-Doctor $0.43 vs mini $0.23 on Verified, $0.64 vs $0.52 on Pro (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00990, fetched 2026-09-21); gate the BRT stage on 'no failing test exists' and cap its steps.

Value-model / LLM-as-judge step selection miscalibrates on agents that synthesize their own tools ('fail to generalize to modern agents that synthesize custom bash scripts as tools', https://arxiv.org/html/2601.22129v2, fetched 2026-09-21) — prefer code heuristics for replay-step choice and ablate any Jev question before consuming it (LLM-JEV-DESIGN §10.4).

Regression-test selection by an LLM is a silent failure point: TRAE 'prompts the LLM to identify a subset most likely to represent true regression tests' (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.23370v1, fetched 2026-09-21). In JevCode the regression scope must be a code fact (PASS_TO_PASS / test discovery), not a model guess.

Terminal-Bench 4.0 is not an iteration target: 'flat agent timeout of 8 hours' (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19), $8-28 per task on vals.ai (fetched 2026-09-21), and it needs Docker/Modal which the reference machine lacks (docs/RESEARCH.md §0.4). Use the checked-in 10 tasks or a TB 2.x mid-range subset for quick loops.

Subprocess-per-action (mini-SWE-agent) cannot drive interactive or long-running programs; a persistent tmux tool (Terminus 2) can but reintroduces 'did it finish?' ambiguity and needs explicit waits (min(duration,60)). Pick per benchmark; do not mix in one run.

The mid-range subset protocol needs prior history: 'approximately five to ten agents must be evaluated on the full benchmark before reduction becomes reliable' (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23749v1, fetched 2026-09-21); use public per-instance results, and remember it preserves ranks, not absolute scores.

Official boards are hard to read programmatically and gated: swebench.com and tbench.ai leaderboards are JS-rendered (both fetched 2026-09-21 with no rows); Verified/Multilingual submissions require an arXiv/tech report and academic affiliation since 2025-11-18 (docs/research/04, fetched 2026-09-19). Do not plan on an official leaderboard submission as the acceptance test.

Compaction and summaries built by a model can drop the very facts that matter; CCA's fix is to pin the categories (goals, decisions, TODOs, error traces) (https://arxiv.org/html/2512.10398, fetched 2026-09-21). In JevCode build the summary from harness facts; Jev must never be asked to write it (design rule: Jev does not build text).

Do not put Jev on a mission-critical path: every mechanism above has a code default (first passing candidate, top-k of code ranking, first well-formed proposal), and the llm-sieve arm exists to prove the loop works with zero Jev requests. Consume a Jev question only after the §10.4 ablation shows positive marginal contribution.

Research-time gaps: morphllm.com and artificialanalysis.ai returned HTTP 429/classifier rate limits; the Harbor Terminus-2 doc redirected; the swebench.com bash-only listing 404'd; the mini-swe-agent FAQ lacked cost/step defaults. Claims about opencode's Terminal-Bench standing and vendor-scaffold Verified numbers (~93.9%/95%) come only from WebSearch snippets and are marked [SECONDARY].
